guides.title: Asynchronous replication: two different promises
guides.summary: The write avoids waiting for that replica, but replica reads can lag. Promoting an out-of-date replica after primary failure can lose acknowledged writes. Define acceptable staleness and data loss separately; replication alone does not imply read-after-write consistency.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: The write avoids waiting for that replica, but replica reads can lag. Promoting an out-of-date replica after primary failure can lose acknowledged writes. Define acceptable staleness and data loss separately; replication alone does not imply read-after-write consistency.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: Follow the write through four moments: primary commits, client receives success, replica receives the log, replica replays it. Acknowledging at the second moment leaves the last two unfinished. Distinguish data durability after failover from freshness of reads during healthy operation.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: At 10:00:00 an account name becomes Ada on the primary. The reply arrives at 10:00:00.020, but replica replay finishes at 10:00:00.300. A read at 10:00:00.100 can return the old name. If the primary is irrecoverably lost before transfer, promoting that replica can also lose the change. These are two different failure stories.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Route freshness-sensitive reads to the authoritative node, or wait for a specific replication position.
Measure replica lag and test failover loss; average healthy-state lag is not a maximum-loss guarantee.
Choose asynchronous replication when lower write latency and replica unavailability tolerance justify the stated loss window.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: Explain why “three copies” says little without the acknowledgement policy. What happens if the primary dies immediately after success?

guides.title: Synchronous replication: define the acknowledgement
guides.summary: Specify which replicas acknowledge and whether acknowledgement means receipt, durable storage, or application. Waiting adds latency and can block commits when required replicas are unavailable. Durable acknowledgement does not mean every replica can already serve the new value.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: Specify which replicas acknowledge and whether acknowledgement means receipt, durable storage, or application. Waiting adds latency and can block commits when required replicas are unavailable. Durable acknowledgement does not mean every replica can already serve the new value.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: A synchronous commit waits for a configured set of replicas to reach a specified point. Receipt in memory, durable log flush, and replay for queries are different points. Requiring more remote acknowledgements can strengthen a failure guarantee while increasing latency and the number of failures that block progress.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: Imagine A is the primary and B and C are replicas. A waits for B to flush its log, then replies. B can recover the log after a crash, but a query on B may wait for replay. C was not required at all. “A synchronous write” therefore does not justify sending an immediate read to arbitrary C.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Name which node failures you intend to survive. Separate local durability, remote durability, and read visibility.
A slow required replica can increase tail latency. Decide whether to block or deliberately weaken the policy during failures.
Synchronous replicas still do not replace backups against application deletion or corruption.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: Draw the acknowledgement boundary. Which exact replica can safely serve the next read, and under what replay condition?

guides.title: Partition keys: distribution versus hot traffic
guides.summary: Hashing spreads distinct keys, not the requests for one key. A heavily accessed key can dominate one partition even when key counts are balanced. Evaluate traffic and item sizes per key, plus secondary-index access patterns, rather than relying on aggregate table capacity.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: Hashing spreads distinct keys, not the requests for one key. A heavily accessed key can dominate one partition even when key counts are balanced. Evaluate traffic and item sizes per key, plus secondary-index access patterns, rather than relying on aggregate table capacity.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: A partition function chooses where a key lives. It does not divide the work for a single key. Compare per-key request frequency, bytes, and write contention; uniform counts of stored keys can coexist with extremely uneven traffic.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: One million customers are evenly hashed across 100 partitions. One customer sends 40% of all writes. Its partition receives those writes plus roughly its normal share of the remaining traffic. Adding cold customers changes key-count balance but does nothing to that hot customer.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Cache repeated reads where freshness permits; write hotspots usually need a different key or data model.
Bucket time-series writes or add shards only if readers can locate or merge the pieces.
A secondary index can introduce its own hot key even when the base-table key is balanced.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: Ask whether the hot unit is an entire tenant, one record, or a global counter. Why can only some of these be split without changing semantics?

guides.title: Indexes: pay on writes to save selected reads
guides.summary: Indexes accelerate suitable lookups but require storage and maintenance when data changes. Choose them from important access patterns and verify the query plan. A planner may prefer a sequential scan when the index would not save enough work; an unused index still imposes costs.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: Indexes accelerate suitable lookups but require storage and maintenance when data changes. Choose them from important access patterns and verify the query plan. A planner may prefer a sequential scan when the index would not save enough work; an unused index still imposes costs.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: A B-tree maintains sorted searchable entries pointing toward rows. A useful index narrows the candidate range before fetching data. Every indexed insert, delete, and relevant update may also maintain this extra structure, and the structure consumes cache and storage.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: An orders table is commonly queried by tenant and recent creation time. An index aligned with that access path can avoid scanning other tenants. An index on an unfiltered notes field does not help that query, yet all incoming orders still pay its maintenance cost.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Start with a high-value query, its predicates, ordering, output columns, and measured plan.
Low-selectivity queries can legitimately scan. An index seek followed by many random row lookups may be worse.
Write throughput, storage, vacuum or maintenance, and memory pressure belong in the decision.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: Given three candidate indexes, explain which measured access pattern each serves and what redundant work it adds.

guides.title: Transactions do not automatically protect every invariant
guides.summary: No. PostgreSQL’s default Read Committed isolation gives each statement a snapshot, so concurrent transactions can still violate a multi-statement business invariant. Use suitable constraints, locking, or Serializable isolation for the invariant. Serializable transactions can abort on conflicts; retry the entire transaction, including its reads.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: No. PostgreSQL’s default Read Committed isolation gives each statement a snapshot, so concurrent transactions can still violate a multi-statement business invariant. Use suitable constraints, locking, or Serializable isolation for the invariant. Serializable transactions can abort on conflicts; retry the entire transaction, including its reads.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: Atomicity says a transaction commits all its database changes or none. Isolation controls what concurrent transactions can observe and how conflicts are handled. Read Committed does not turn a multi-statement decision into a serial execution of the entire business operation.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: A toy roster requires at least one doctor on call. Two transactions each read that two doctors are present. Each removes a different doctor and commits. Individual row updates can succeed while the cross-row invariant fails. A transaction around each sequence was not sufficient.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Prefer an enforceable constraint when the invariant can be expressed by the database.
Otherwise serialize the relevant decision with appropriate locks or use Serializable with whole-transaction retry.
Keep network calls outside held database locks when possible; they extend contention and do not join database atomicity.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: Name the invariant before naming an isolation level. Explain which concurrent interleaving your solution prevents.

guides.title: Cache-aside and its stale-fill race
guides.summary: No. A miss loads the database value into the cache, but invalidation races or writes outside the cache path can leave stale entries. Update the database before invalidating its cached value, while recognizing that this order alone does not eliminate every race. Choose TTLs and stronger coordination according to the freshness requirement.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: No. A miss loads the database value into the cache, but invalidation races or writes outside the cache path can leave stale entries. Update the database before invalidating its cached value, while recognizing that this order alone does not eliminate every race. Choose TTLs and stronger coordination according to the freshness requirement.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: The application checks a cache; on a miss it reads the source and stores the result. Writes change the source and typically invalidate the cached copy. A TTL bounds residence after a fill, but does not itself coordinate readers and writers.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: Reader R misses and reads version 1. Writer W commits version 2 and deletes the cache entry. R now stores version 1. The recommended database-then-invalidate order did not prevent this in-flight stale fill. A five-minute TTL may leave version 1 visible for five more minutes.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Use cache-aside for read-heavy data with an explicit freshness allowance.
Versioned keys or version-aware writes can avoid overwriting newer state; coordination adds complexity.
For strict reads, bypass this cache or use a design with a stronger verified consistency contract.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: Walk through the race using R and W. What does your freshness requirement permit, and what does your TTL actually bound?

guides.title: Idempotency keys represent an intention
guides.summary: Two intentional operations can have identical parameters. A stable operation ID distinguishes one operation’s retries from a new operation. Scope the ID to the caller and operation, reject conflicting reuse, and retain the outcome for the supported retry window. Recording the ID and applying the effect must be atomic or recoverable.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: Two intentional operations can have identical parameters. A stable operation ID distinguishes one operation’s retries from a new operation. Scope the ID to the caller and operation, reject conflicting reuse, and retain the outcome for the supported retry window. Recording the ID and applying the effect must be atomic or recoverable.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: An operation key identifies one logical request across transport retries. Store its request fingerprint, status, and outcome. The key namespace must include the relevant caller or tenant. Same key plus conflicting input should fail rather than silently reuse a different result.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: A shopper intentionally buys the same book twice on different days. Both bodies are identical, but the operation keys are K1 and K2. A network retry of the first purchase reuses K1. Deduplicating by body hash would incorrectly merge the two intentional purchases.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Use a unique database constraint so two concurrent requests cannot both claim the key.
Make the effect and durable idempotency record atomic, or persist a resumable state machine that can reconcile uncertainty.
Define retention, in-progress responses, and whether failures are retained. A retry after expiry may be a new operation.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: Explain the crash between performing an effect and saving its result. How is a later retry resolved?

sources.title: Amazon Builders’ Library: Making retries safe with idempotent APIs

guides.title: Retries need a deadline and a spread
guides.summary: Backoff spaces out one client’s retries; jitter spreads retries from many clients so they do not return together. Also cap attempts or elapsed time and retry only appropriate failures. Backoff with jitter reduces synchronization, but unlimited retries can still overload a dependency.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: Backoff spaces out one client’s retries; jitter spreads retries from many clients so they do not return together. Also cap attempts or elapsed time and retry only appropriate failures. Backoff with jitter reduces synchronization, but unlimited retries can still overload a dependency.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: Exponential backoff increases the delay between attempts. Jitter varies delays between callers, breaking synchronized bursts. Neither makes a permanently invalid request useful, and retries consume real capacity from a dependency that may already be failing.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: For attempt n, one illustrative full-jitter delay is uniform(0, min(2 seconds, 100 milliseconds × 2^n)). Ten thousand callers do not all wake at precisely 100, 200, and 400 milliseconds. Still stop at the overall deadline and use the same operation key for a retried create.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Separate connection, per-attempt, and overall operation deadlines. Account for work already attempted.
Retry only classified transient failures and safe or idempotent operations; honor service guidance such as Retry-After.
A bounded retry budget and concurrency limit protect a recovering dependency.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: What happens if the first attempt succeeds but its reply is lost? Backoff is not the answer to that correctness question.

sources.title: Amazon Builders’ Library: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter

guides.title: A queue buys time, not processing capacity
guides.summary: No. A queue buffers bursts and separates intake from processing, but backlog grows if average arrival rate exceeds completion rate. Monitor backlog age and depth. Increase safe processing capacity, limit intake, or shed work; unrestricted worker scaling can simply overload the downstream database.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: No. A queue buffers bursts and separates intake from processing, but backlog grows if average arrival rate exceeds completion rate. Monitor backlog age and depth. Increase safe processing capacity, limit intake, or shed work; unrestricted worker scaling can simply overload the downstream database.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: Backlog changes by arrivals minus completions. A queue absorbs a temporary mismatch and lets workers run independently of request intake. When the long-term arrival rate exceeds sustainable completion rate, backlog and waiting time keep increasing.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: A toy worker fleet completes 80 jobs per second while intake stays at 100. After ten minutes the queue has added about 12,000 jobs. Adding workers helps only if the next bottleneck, such as the database, can sustain the larger load.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Monitor oldest-message age as well as depth; the user cares how long their work is waiting.
Bound intake, worker concurrency, and storage. Choose rejection, deferred admission, or lower-priority shedding deliberately.
Handle poison messages with bounded retries and inspection rather than endlessly blocking useful work.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: After a ten-minute spike ends, how much spare completion capacity exists to drain its backlog, and how long will recovery take?

sources.title: Microsoft Azure Architecture Center: Queue-Based Load Leveling Pattern

guides.title: Consumer acknowledgement creates a crash window
guides.summary: Acknowledging first risks losing the work if the consumer crashes before completing it. Acknowledging afterward permits redelivery if the work commits but the acknowledgement is lost. The latter supports at-least-once processing when delivery is retried, so consumers must tolerate duplicates.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: Acknowledging first risks losing the work if the consumer crashes before completing it. Acknowledging afterward permits redelivery if the work commits but the acknowledgement is lost. The latter supports at-least-once processing when delivery is retried, so consumers must tolerate duplicates.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: The broker needs evidence that it can stop tracking a delivery. Acknowledging before the business effect risks lost work. Committing first and acknowledging second creates a duplicate window. At-least-once delivery therefore needs a duplicate-safe effect.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: A worker receives message M, adds a loyalty credit, commits, and crashes before ack. The broker later redelivers M. A transactional unique processed-message record lets the next worker recognize that the credit was already committed.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Publisher confirmation is a separate leg; it does not prove consumer work completed.
Acknowledge only after durable success under the intended business contract.
Bound unacknowledged deliveries so a slow consumer does not accumulate unlimited work in memory.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: Draw the crash immediately before and immediately after each step. Which failures cause loss and which cause duplicates?

guides.title: Tail latency: measure the slow experience
guides.summary: A fast majority can hide a slow tail. Inspect a latency distribution and relevant percentiles, and distinguish successful from failed requests. A page that depends on several services can expose users to slow outliers frequently. Define the measurement window and measure the end-to-end user operation as well as dependencies.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: A fast majority can hide a slow tail. Inspect a latency distribution and relevant percentiles, and distinguish successful from failed requests. A page that depends on several services can expose users to slow outliers frequently. Define the measurement window and measure the end-to-end user operation as well as dependencies.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: A percentile describes a point in a measured latency distribution. The mean can stay small while a meaningful fraction of users wait seconds. Fan-out makes slow dependencies especially important because the user operation often waits for its slowest required branch.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: Of 100 toy requests, 99 finish in 10 ms and one in 5,000 ms. The mean is 59.9 ms, but the unlucky user waited five seconds. If many independent branches each have a slow tail, an operation needing all branches encounters an outlier more frequently.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Measure end-to-end latency, including queueing, and name the window and eligible requests.
Separate successes and failures; fast failures can make a latency metric look deceptively healthy.
Percentiles cannot generally be averaged across hosts. Merge suitable distributions or histograms.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: If p50 is stable and p99 doubles, investigate saturation, lock contention, pauses, slow I/O, and request mix before adding arbitrary replicas.

sources.title: Google SRE: Monitoring Distributed Systems

guides.title: Capacity belongs to a workload and an SLO
guides.summary: Request costs differ. Tie the rate to a workload mix, payload sizes, and latency target, then measure the limiting resources such as CPU, memory, network, or storage I/O. A change in query mix can invalidate a request-rate estimate even if total traffic is unchanged.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: Request costs differ. Tie the rate to a workload mix, payload sizes, and latency target, then measure the limiting resources such as CPU, memory, network, or storage I/O. A change in query mix can invalidate a request-rate estimate even if total traffic is unchanged.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: A request is not a unit of equal cost. Throughput depends on query work, payloads, CPU time, I/O, concurrency, and required latency. As utilization approaches a limiting resource, queueing can increase latency long before outright errors appear.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: A read endpoint serves cached 1 KB objects cheaply. A report endpoint scans millions of rows and serializes 10 MB. “1,000 requests per second” predicts little until the mix is known. A load test that warms every cache can miss a cold-start collapse.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Estimate bytes, CPU or I/O per operation, peak concurrency, and fan-out; then validate with a realistic load test.
Include headroom for node loss, bursts, background maintenance, and uneven tenants.
Report capacity at a latency and error target, rather than at the point where the server barely avoids crashing.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: Which resource saturates first, and what signal would prove that diagnosis rather than simply correlate with it?

sources.title: Google SRE: Handling Overload

guides.title: SLOs turn reliability into a measurable decision
guides.summary: Define what counts as a good event and the measurement window. The allowed fraction of bad events is the error budget: a 99.9% request-success target allows 0.1% failures among eligible requests. Agree on actions when the budget is consumed, such as prioritizing reliability work or limiting risky releases.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: Define what counts as a good event and the measurement window. The allowed fraction of bad events is the error budget: a 99.9% request-success target allows 0.1% failures among eligible requests. Agree on actions when the budget is consumed, such as prioritizing reliability work or limiting risky releases.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: An SLI is the observed indicator, an SLO is its target, and an error budget is the permitted bad portion over the chosen window. Select eligible events and the definition of good carefully so the metric represents user experience.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: For a toy month with 2,000,000 eligible operations and a 99.9% success SLO, the budget is 2,000 bad operations. If 1,500 fail in the first week, 500 remain under that simple event-based accounting. This is not automatically equivalent to a fixed number of downtime minutes.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Define latency and correctness goals where “HTTP 200” alone misses a bad experience.
Choose alerting and release policies before an incident; use consumption rate to distinguish urgent loss from small noise.
Do not promise 100% without confronting the cost and the meaning of dependencies.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: What decision changes when the budget is being exhausted? A target with no operational consequence is only a dashboard number.

sources.title: Google SRE Workbook: Implementing SLOs

guides.title: RPO and RTO: loss and downtime are different
guides.summary: RPO limits acceptable data loss, expressed as a time window. RTO limits acceptable time to restore service. A low RPO drives backup or replication frequency; a low RTO drives recovery readiness and automation. Set them from business impact and dependencies, then validate the design with recovery tests.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: RPO limits acceptable data loss, expressed as a time window. RTO limits acceptable time to restore service. A low RPO drives backup or replication frequency; a low RTO drives recovery readiness and automation. Set them from business impact and dependencies, then validate the design with recovery tests.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: RPO describes how old the recovered state may be relative to failure; RTO describes the acceptable recovery duration. A frequent backup can improve the first while leaving a slow manual restore for the second.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: A toy service permits 15 minutes of data loss and one hour of downtime. Hourly backups alone miss the RPO. Five-minute backups might meet that loss goal, but a three-hour restore misses the RTO. Measure the complete path from detecting failure to restored useful service.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Include database, identity, secrets, DNS, object storage, and external dependencies in recovery exercises.
Replicas can faithfully copy corruption or accidental deletion; retain recoverable historical state.
Choose objectives from user impact and cost, then test actual restoration instead of inferring it from a backup-success email.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: If a restore drill exceeds RTO, which step dominates: provisioning, data transfer, replay, validation, or traffic cutover?

sources.title: AWS Reliability Pillar: Define recovery objectives for downtime and data loss

guides.title: One database transaction, one atomic boundary
guides.summary: It makes the database changes commit together or roll back together, preventing an observer from seeing a partly committed operation. This is useful when the related state fits one database transaction. An HTTP call or message publication outside that transaction does not become atomic merely because the database work is transactional.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: It makes the database changes commit together or roll back together, preventing an observer from seeing a partly committed operation. This is useful when the related state fits one database transaction. An HTTP call or message publication outside that transaction does not become atomic merely because the database work is transactional.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: A transaction groups related changes so committed state does not contain only half the operation. Constraints and suitable isolation are still required for correctness under concurrency. Database rollback cannot unsend an external HTTP request.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: In a toy order database, insert the order and its order lines in one transaction. If a line violates a constraint, roll back the order too. If sending a confirmation email fails after commit, the database cannot roll back the email system; record pending notification work durably.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Keep transactions short and avoid user interaction while locks are held.
Handle the commit-result-unknown case after a connection failure using a stable business operation ID.
Use an outbox to connect committed state to eventual message publication.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: List every effect in the operation and mark which can actually join this transaction. Treat the remaining effects explicitly.

guides.title: Composite indexes follow the access path
guides.summary: A composite index on (tenant_id, created_at): the leading equality narrows the tenant, then the range narrows its records. Verify with the actual query plan and data distribution. Queries filtering only created_at may need a different index; do not assume either that this index is ideal or that it is never usable.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: A composite index on (tenant_id, created_at): the leading equality narrows the tenant, then the range narrows its records. Verify with the actual query plan and data distribution. Queries filtering only created_at may need a different index; do not assume either that this index is ideal or that it is never usable.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: A composite B-tree orders by the first key, then the next within equal preceding keys. Equality on tenant followed by a time range naturally fits (tenant_id, created_at). Additional output columns may change whether row lookups are needed.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: For tenant 7 and dates from October 1 through October 2, the index can locate that tenant’s slice and walk the relevant dates. A query for all tenants on October 1 is a different access path. Test its plan rather than asserting the existing index can never help.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Use realistic cardinality and skew when checking estimated and actual plans.
Add a unique tiebreaker when ordering and pagination need a stable sequence.
An index has write and space costs even when a particular planner chooses a scan.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: Write the exact WHERE and ORDER BY before proposing an index. What changes if the equality column becomes a range?

guides.title: Redis cache policy under memory pressure
guides.summary: Set a memory limit and an eviction policy that fits the access pattern, then monitor hits, misses, and evictions. LRU or LFU policies can evict reusable entries; noeviction instead rejects writes that need more memory. TTL expiration and memory-pressure eviction are separate mechanisms. Leave room for process overhead and replication or persistence buffers.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: Set a memory limit and an eviction policy that fits the access pattern, then monitor hits, misses, and evictions. LRU or LFU policies can evict reusable entries; noeviction instead rejects writes that need more memory. TTL expiration and memory-pressure eviction are separate mechanisms. Leave room for process overhead and replication or persistence buffers.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: TTL expiration removes keys because time has passed. Eviction removes eligible keys because the memory policy needs room. LRU approximates recent use; LFU approximates frequent use. A noeviction policy can reject memory-growing writes instead of discarding cache entries.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: A toy cache holds catalog pages with one-hour TTLs. A sudden import exceeds its memory budget after five minutes. Entries may be evicted before their TTLs expire. If the application assumes TTL guarantees residency, its miss traffic can unexpectedly hit the database.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: Monitor used memory, process overhead, hit rate, misses, evictions, and rejected writes.
Leave room for replication and persistence buffers rather than assigning all machine RAM to data.
Cache contents must be safe to recompute or lose under the chosen policy.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: Explain how you would load-test a cold cache and prevent an eviction spiral from saturating the source database.

sources.title: Redis: Key eviction

guides.title: Redis success is not one universal durability guarantee
guides.summary: It depends on persistence and failure mode. With persistence disabled, memory loss loses the dataset. RDB snapshots can lose changes since the last snapshot; AOF durability depends on its fsync policy. Choose and test a loss window appropriate to the data rather than treating a cache acknowledgement as durable database commit.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: It depends on persistence and failure mode. With persistence disabled, memory loss loses the dataset. RDB snapshots can lose changes since the last snapshot; AOF durability depends on its fsync policy. Choose and test a loss window appropriate to the data rather than treating a cache acknowledgement as durable database commit.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: Redis can serve memory-resident state with different persistence configurations. Snapshots represent discrete points in time; append-only logging has a synchronization policy. Durability also depends on the failure you are considering, such as process exit versus host or disk loss.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: In a toy deployment, a snapshot at 12:00 is the only persisted copy and the machine fails at 12:08. Writes acknowledged during those eight minutes may disappear on restore. Reconstructible cache entries tolerate this; an authoritative ledger probably does not.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: State the maximum acceptable loss window and validate the selected persistence and replication behavior.
Test restore, not just backup creation. Monitor persistence failures and resource pressure.
Do not treat replication, disk persistence, and historical backups as interchangeable protections.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: Which data in Redis is authoritative, and what exactly reconstructs it if every memory copy disappears?

guides.title: Kafka ordering is a partition-level tool
guides.summary: Use customer ID so that customer’s records share a partition under a stable partitioning scheme. Ordering is partition-scoped, and application processing must preserve the order it needs. A busy customer can create a hot partition. Changing partition count or spreading one customer across partitions requires an explicit ordering strategy.

sections.title: Answer the card
paragraphs: Use customer ID so that customer’s records share a partition under a stable partitioning scheme. Ordering is partition-scoped, and application processing must preserve the order it needs. A busy customer can create a hot partition. Changing partition count or spreading one customer across partitions requires an explicit ordering strategy.

sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: Records in a partition have an ordered log position. Keying by customer can place that customer’s events together under a stable partitioner. Consumer application code must still avoid reordering the business effects, such as launching all deliveries concurrently.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: Customer 42 creates event A then event B. Both reach partition 3 in that order. If a worker starts two asynchronous handlers and B finishes first, downstream effects can still occur out of order. The log’s order did not serialize the handlers.

sections.title: Tradeoffs and failure modes
bullets: A hot customer can dominate a single partition, limiting per-customer parallelism.
Changing partition count can change key routing, so plan migration when cross-change order matters.
Define whether the requirement is per customer, per order, or global; global ordering imposes a much tighter bottleneck.

sections.title: Explain it out loud
paragraphs: Where is order created, persisted, and preserved during retries? Does the destination accept sequence numbers or reject stale updates?

guides.title: Kafka groups: partitions bound traditional ownership
guides.summary: No, assuming they subscribe only to that topic: at most six can hold assignments because one partition has one consumer owner within a traditional group at a time. More consumers can provide standby capacity. Adding partitions changes the scaling and key-placement tradeoffs; this rule does not describe Kafka share groups.

paragraphs: No, assuming they subscribe only to that topic: at most six can hold assignments because one partition has one consumer owner within a traditional group at a time. sections.title: How it works
paragraphs: Insert a unique message-processing marker and apply the database effect inside the same transaction. If both commit, a retry sees the marker. If the transaction rolls back, neither remains. The unique constraint handles simultaneous duplicate attempts.

guides.summary: SELECT chooses the output columns and expressions. WHERE decides which source rows survive. AS names an output expression. Listing required columns makes the result contract clearer than SELECT *.

sections.title: Build the idea
paragraphs: Read a simple query as FROM the source, WHERE eligible rows, SELECT output expressions, ORDER BY the final sequence. That is a useful logical model, not a promise about the physical execution order. Expressions run per output row unless aggregation changes the grain.

guides.title: 04 · ORDER BY, ties, and limiting rows
guides.summary: Limiting rows does not define which rows come first. Use ORDER BY for the intended order and a unique tie-breaker for deterministic results. SQL Server uses TOP or OFFSET/FETCH; SQLite uses LIMIT.

guides.title: 05 · NULL and three-valued logic
guides.summary: Comparisons with NULL produce UNKNOWN rather than TRUE or FALSE. WHERE keeps only TRUE. Test missing values with IS NULL or IS NOT NULL; use COALESCE only when a replacement matches the business meaning.

guides.title: 09 · LEFT JOIN, missing matches, and filter placement
guides.summary: LEFT JOIN supplies NULL right-side columns for unmatched left rows. A right-side comparison in WHERE often rejects those NULL rows. Put a matching-condition filter in ON when the left rows must remain even without qualifying matches.

guides.title: 10 · Join multiplicity and avoiding double counting
guides.summary: The order’s total repeats once per matching line. Summing at that expanded grain counts some orders more than once. Aggregate at the intended grain before joining, or sum line amounts when that is the actual measure.

sections.title: Recall target
paragraphs: The order’s total repeats once per matching line. Summing at that expanded grain counts some orders more than once. Aggregate at the intended grain before joining, or sum line amounts when that is the actual measure.

sections.title: Build the idea
paragraphs: Name the grain of every intermediate result. Orders is one row per order; the order-to-line join is one row per line. When joining two one-to-many child sets, the result can multiply both sides. DISTINCT amounts are not a repair because separate orders can legitimately have identical totals.

       SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_cents) AS line_total_cents

guides.title: 15 · Running totals and explicit window frames
guides.summary: It explicitly sums from the first row through the current row in the window’s sequence. A deterministic order plus a ROWS frame gives row-by-row accumulation. Default frames and peer rows can produce surprising totals when ordering values tie.

sections.title: Dialect and verification

guides.title: 24 · Offset versus keyset pagination
guides.summary: It stores the last seen ordering values, then asks for rows after that position. A unique tie-breaker makes the order total, so equal timestamps do not create ambiguous page boundaries. Offset skips a count of rows and can become costly or shift under concurrent changes.

sections.title: Recall target
paragraphs: It stores the last seen ordering values, then asks for rows after that position. A unique tie-breaker makes the order total, so equal timestamps do not create ambiguous page boundaries. Offset skips a count of rows and can become costly or shift under concurrent changes.

sections.title: Build the idea
paragraphs: For descending (ordered_on, order_id), the next page has an earlier date or the same date with a smaller ID. Match the comparison direction to the sort. Use an opaque validated cursor in an API, keep filters stable, and consider snapshot semantics if a consistent whole-list traversal matters.

sections.title: Worked query
sections.code:
SELECT order_id, ordered_on
FROM Orders
WHERE ordered_on < '2026-02-02'
   OR (ordered_on = '2026-02-02' AND order_id < 105)
ORDER BY ordered_on DESC, order_id DESC
LIMIT 2;

sections.title: Expected result on the shared toy data
Read the result
paragraphs: The first page was 106 then 105. Its last position is (2026-02-02, 105). The next page returns 104 then 103. Using only the date would mishandle ties at the boundary in a page that splits same-date rows.

sections.title: Common mistakes
bullets: Keyset pagination is not automatic snapshot isolation; edits to sort keys can still affect traversal.
Offset supports direct page-number jumps more naturally, while keyset suits sequential navigation.
Always enforce tenant and other filters again; a cursor is not an authorization token.

sections.title: Try it before revealing your answer
paragraphs: If page size is one and the first row is 106, what is the next row? Expected: 105, using the same date and smaller ID branch.

sections.title: Dialect and verification
paragraphs: Executed SQLite version uses LIMIT 2. SQL Server uses SELECT TOP (2) with the same WHERE and ORDER BY. SQL Server OFFSET 2 ROWS FETCH NEXT 2 ROWS ONLY is an alternative offset approach, but is not used in this tested query.

guides.title: 25 · UNION, UNION ALL, and combining result sets
guides.summary: UNION combines compatible result sets and removes duplicate complete rows. UNION ALL keeps duplicates and avoids that deduplication requirement. Use ALL when duplicates are meaningful or the inputs are known to be disjoint.

sections.title: Recall target
paragraphs: UNION combines compatible result sets and removes duplicate complete rows. UNION ALL keeps duplicates and avoids that deduplication requirement. Use ALL when duplicates are meaningful or the inputs are known to be disjoint.

sections.title: Build the idea
paragraphs: A join combines columns through related row pairs. A union stacks rows from separate queries with compatible column counts and types. The first query supplies result column names. Add final ordering to the combined result rather than assuming each input’s order is preserved.

sections.title: Worked query
sections.code:
SELECT city FROM Customers WHERE customer_id IN (1, 2)
UNION
SELECT city FROM Customers WHERE customer_id = 4
ORDER BY city;

sections.title: Expected result on the shared toy data
sections.code:
city
Oslo
Paris

sections.title: Read the result
paragraphs: The first input contains Oslo and Paris. The second contains Oslo. UNION outputs Oslo once. UNION ALL would produce Oslo twice and Paris once, with explicit ordering needed for display. This deduplication is about whole rows, so adding customer_id would change which rows are duplicates.

sections.title: Common mistakes
bullets: Do not use UNION to hide an accidental overlap until you understand why the same business row appears twice.
INTERSECT and EXCEPT are useful set comparisons to learn next; duplicate and NULL semantics deserve deliberate tests.
Type conversion rules can differ across engines; align output types rather than relying on surprising coercion.

sections.title: Try it before revealing your answer
paragraphs: Change UNION to UNION ALL and predict the ordered cities: Oslo, Oslo, Paris. Explain why this is different from a join.

guides.title: Interview delivery: from requirements to failure analysis
guides.summary: Build a coherent end-to-end design before adding specialized infrastructure. Start with the user operations and measurable constraints, then show the state, API, request paths, and failure tradeoffs.

sections.title: Core idea
paragraphs: Build a coherent end-to-end design before adding specialized infrastructure. Start with the user operations and measurable constraints, then show the state, API, request paths, and failure tradeoffs.

sections.title: Reason through the mechanism
paragraphs: For a toy photo-processing service, define upload, processing status, and download. Ask about file size, upload rate, processing latency, retention, authorization, and whether lost jobs are acceptable. Separate essential requirements from optional editing features. Use estimates when they change storage, bandwidth, worker capacity, or design choices.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: One initial design is an API that authorizes an upload, object storage for bytes, a database for metadata, a durable queue for processing intent, and workers that publish a result. Trace one successful upload all the way to a retrievable result before discussing multi-region operation.

sections.title: Tradeoffs
bullets: Give each box a role and each arrow a protocol or operation. Name the source of truth.
Deep-dive on the hardest requirement: duplicate delivery, hot workloads, large files, or strict freshness. Explain the cost of your choice.
Close by testing the design against failures: lost replies, worker crash, unavailable dependency, and recovery.

sections.title: Practice aloud
paragraphs: Practice a 35-minute design aloud. Reserve time for one complete request trace and one failure trace. Record assumptions and invite correction instead of memorizing a vendor diagram.

guides.title: Consistency models and CAP without slogans
guides.summary: During a network partition, a distributed system cannot guarantee both linearizable operations and a successful response to every request at every non-failing node. State the operation and failure conditions rather than saying “pick any two”.

sections.title: Core idea
paragraphs: During a network partition, a distributed system cannot guarantee both linearizable operations and a successful response to every request at every non-failing node. State the operation and failure conditions rather than saying “pick any two”.

sections.title: Reason through the mechanism
paragraphs: Linearizability treats each operation as taking effect at one point between invocation and response, respecting completed-operation order. Eventual consistency permits temporary divergence with convergence under suitable conditions. Session guarantees such as read-your-writes are narrower and often useful. CAP consistency is not the C in ACID.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: Two disconnected regions each have the last remaining toy ticket. Accepting sales independently risks overselling. Refusing or deferring the sale on a side that cannot establish authority sacrifices availability for that operation. A public catalog description can tolerate a different choice from ticket purchase.

sections.title: Tradeoffs
bullets: Availability in CAP is a formal response guarantee, not a monthly uptime percentage.
Healthy-network latency and consistency tradeoffs still exist; CAP does not choose your ordinary read strategy.
Define conflict resolution, authority, and recovery after connectivity returns.

sections.title: Practice aloud
paragraphs: For profile display, stock reservation, and analytics counters, name the consistency needed and what users see during a partition.

guides.title: Rate limiting, token buckets, and admission control
guides.summary: A rate limit bounds work admitted over time. A concurrency limit bounds work in flight. Both may be needed because slow requests can occupy resources even at a modest arrival rate.

sections.title: Core idea
paragraphs: A rate limit bounds work admitted over time. A concurrency limit bounds work in flight. Both may be needed because slow requests can occupy resources even at a modest arrival rate.

sections.title: Reason through the mechanism
paragraphs: A token bucket replenishes tokens at a set rate up to a capacity. An operation spends tokens; a full bucket permits a bounded burst. Fixed windows are simple but allow boundary bursts. Sliding approaches improve smoothness with additional state or approximation. Choose the key by the intended fairness unit, such as tenant or API credential.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: A toy API allows 10 requests per second with a 20-token capacity. After idle time it can accept a burst of 20, then roughly the refill rate. If each request holds a database connection for five seconds, that rate can still create too many concurrent connections, so add a separate concurrency gate.

sections.title: Tradeoffs
bullets: A per-process limiter’s total allowance grows when the fleet grows unless coordinated or allocated.
Decide fail-open versus fail-closed behavior for limiter-store failure based on the endpoint’s consequences.
Reject clearly, bound queues, and prevent retries from immediately undoing the protection.

sections.title: Practice aloud
paragraphs: Explain which limit protects fairness, which protects downstream capacity, and how you prevent one tenant from consuming all shared slots.

guides.title: Load balancing, health checks, and stateless services
guides.summary: A load balancer routes traffic across targets. It can improve distribution and failure handling, but it does not make shared dependencies scale or turn local session state into durable shared state.

sections.title: Core idea
paragraphs: A load balancer routes traffic across targets. It can improve distribution and failure handling, but it does not make shared dependencies scale or turn local session state into durable shared state.

sections.title: Reason through the mechanism
paragraphs: Layer-4 routing operates around transport connections; layer-7 routing understands application protocol properties such as HTTP paths and headers. Health checks select eligible targets, while connection draining lets ongoing work finish during removal. Long-lived connections and uneven request costs complicate simple round-robin assumptions.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: A toy API runs on four instances behind a load balancer. If login sessions exist only in one instance’s memory, a later request routed elsewhere can appear logged out. Store sessions appropriately or use a deliberate verifiable stateless token contract. Sticky routing can hide the problem until that instance fails.

sections.title: Tradeoffs
bullets: Separate liveness from readiness so starting or overloaded instances are not given work they cannot serve.
A database can remain the bottleneck after adding application replicas.
Keep enough spare capacity for one target to fail and test reconnect behavior for long-lived clients.

sections.title: Practice aloud
paragraphs: Describe what happens to in-flight requests, new requests, and per-user state when one instance is removed.

guides.title: Data modeling from access patterns and invariants
guides.summary: Choose a data model by the facts that must remain correct and the operations that must be efficient. A product label such as SQL or NoSQL is not a substitute for keys, queries, constraints, and a consistency contract.

sections.title: Core idea
paragraphs: Choose a data model by the facts that must remain correct and the operations that must be efficient. A product label such as SQL or NoSQL is not a substitute for keys, queries, constraints, and a consistency contract.

sections.title: Reason through the mechanism
paragraphs: Start with entities and their relationships, then list important reads and writes. Normalize changing facts to avoid accidental duplication. Denormalized or derived views can make reads cheap, but require an update and reconciliation strategy. Decide what is authoritative and what can be rebuilt.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: A toy order system stores order headers and lines transactionally, keeps binary receipts in object storage, and builds a searchable order projection asynchronously. Search results may lag; opening the authoritative order can show current state. The search index is not the sole record of the purchase.

sections.title: Tradeoffs
bullets: State partition keys, secondary access paths, and expected skew before choosing a distributed store.
Denormalization changes write complexity and repair needs; it is not simply faster data.
Model deletion, retention, migrations, and tenant isolation alongside happy-path queries.

guides.title: Polling, SSE, WebSockets, and reconnecting clients
guides.summary: Choose the simplest delivery mechanism that meets update frequency and direction needs. Polling is straightforward, SSE streams server-to-client events, and WebSockets support bidirectional messaging. The connection alone is not durable event delivery.

sections.title: Core idea
paragraphs: Choose the simplest delivery mechanism that meets update frequency and direction needs. Polling is straightforward, SSE streams server-to-client events, and WebSockets support bidirectional messaging. The connection alone is not durable event delivery.

sections.title: Reason through the mechanism
paragraphs: Persistent connections require lifecycle management: authentication, idle timeouts, heartbeats, reconnect backoff, per-client buffers, and slow-consumer policy. Server-side producers must route updates to the process holding the appropriate connection. Durable state and replay or resynchronization handle disconnections.

sections.title: Worked scenario
paragraphs: A toy export-progress page can poll every few seconds or receive one-way SSE status updates. A collaborative editor has frequent bidirectional interaction and may use WebSockets. In either case, reconnecting after missing updates needs a version or cursor, or a fresh authoritative snapshot.

sections.title: Tradeoffs
bullets: Do not buffer unlimited events for a disconnected or slow client.
A connected socket does not imply a user processed an event. Add application acknowledgements only when the contract needs them.
WebSocket delivery does not solve concurrent document-edit conflict resolution; that is a separate model.

sections.title: Practice aloud
paragraphs: If the client disconnects after event 18 and reconnects after event 25, how does it regain correct state without duplicating business effects?

cards.front: When you assign a class variable or a struct variable in C#, what is copied?
cards.back: Assignment copies the value of the variable. A struct variable carries its fields; a class variable carries an object reference. Two copied references can point at the same object. Ordinary parameters are passed by value; ref changes that parameter-passing contract.

cards.front: Why should fields used by a dictionary key’s equality and hash code stay unchanged?
cards.back: A hash collection chooses a bucket using the key’s hash. Mutating equality-relevant state after insertion can make later lookup search the wrong bucket. Equal keys must have equal hash codes. Use stable keys and an explicit equality policy.

cards.front: How can a .NET program leak memory even though it has garbage collection?
cards.back: GC reclaims managed objects that are no longer reachable. A cache, event handler, static field, or unfinished operation that still references an unnecessary object keeps it alive. GC does not know the application no longer needs it.

cards.front: Why use using even when .NET has garbage collection?
cards.back: GC manages object memory. IDisposable releases owned resources deterministically, such as file handles, streams, or transactions. using ensures Dispose runs when scope exits, including exception paths. Async disposal uses await using for IAsyncDisposable.

cards.front: Why is List<T>.Add amortized O(1) although one Add can be O(n)?
cards.back: Most additions fill spare capacity in constant time. Occasionally the backing array grows and existing elements are copied. Across many additions, geometric growth spreads that copying cost, giving amortized constant-time append. This is not a worst-case latency promise.

cards.front: Does C# string.Length count the characters a user sees?
cards.back: It counts UTF-16 code units. A Unicode scalar value can require two code units, and one displayed text element can contain several scalars. Choose code units, Rune values, or grapheme/text elements based on the actual requirement.

cards.front: Why is double often a poor default for decimal monetary calculations?
cards.back: Binary floating-point cannot exactly represent many decimal fractions. decimal is often a better fit for base-10 quantities, but still needs explicit precision and rounding rules. Integer minor units also work when the currency and scale are defined.

cards.front: What is the difference between a process, a thread, and a Task in .NET?
cards.back: A process is an execution and resource-isolation boundary. A thread is an execution path scheduled by the OS. A Task represents an operation that may complete later; it does not imply a dedicated thread. Async I/O can remain pending without occupying a worker thread.

cards.front: Does marking a C# method async move its work to a background thread?
cards.back: No. The method runs synchronously until it reaches an incomplete await. Await arranges continuation after completion without blocking the caller’s thread. Task.Run explicitly schedules CPU work, but wrapping already-asynchronous I/O in it usually adds needless overhead.

cards.front: What does cancelling a CancellationTokenSource guarantee?
cards.back: It requests cooperative cancellation. Operations must observe the token; cancellation does not forcibly undo completed side effects. Pass tokens through I/O and CPU loops, use a total deadline, and bound concurrent work independently.

cards.front: Why is count++ unsafe when multiple threads update the same count?
cards.back: It combines read, increment, and write. Two threads can read the same old value and overwrite one another. Use Interlocked for a supported atomic operation or a shared lock to protect a larger invariant. Every access participating in the invariant must follow the same protocol.

cards.front: How can two individually correct locks create a deadlock?
cards.back: Thread A holds lock X while waiting for Y; thread B holds Y while waiting for X. Neither can progress. A consistent global lock acquisition order prevents that cycle. Short critical sections, limited nesting, and avoiding blocking waits make the system easier to reason about.

cards.front: What happens before an HTTPS request reaches application code?
cards.back: Typically a name is resolved, a transport connection is established, TLS authenticates the server and protects the connection, then HTTP is exchanged. DNS caching, connection pooling, proxies, and protocol version affect the exact path. HTTP/3 uses QUIC rather than TCP.

cards.front: What does HTTP idempotent mean, and does it mean repeated responses are identical?
cards.back: An idempotent method has the same intended server effect when the same request is repeated. Responses can differ: a repeated DELETE can find the resource already absent. GET is intended to be safe; POST is not inherently idempotent and often needs an application operation key.

cards.front: Why should an API use explicit DTOs instead of serializing database entities directly?
cards.back: DTOs define the public contract independently of persistence. They reduce accidental field disclosure, unwanted client-settable fields, cyclic graphs, and coupling to schema changes. Serialization converts data to a representation; it does not validate permissions or business meaning.

cards.front: What belongs in an API contract beyond an endpoint and JSON shape?
cards.back: Identity and authorization, input constraints, success and error semantics, idempotency, concurrency/version rules, pagination order, consistency expectations, and compatibility policy. A precise contract lets callers recover from failures without guessing.

cards.front: Why can a heavily mocked unit-test suite miss a production database bug?
cards.back: A mock can reproduce assumptions rather than real database behavior. Unit tests isolate logic; integration tests exercise real boundaries such as SQL, transactions, and serialization. Contract tests check producer/consumer agreement. Each catches different failures.

cards.front: How do logs, metrics, traces, and profiles answer different questions?
cards.back: Logs record specific events, metrics summarize measurements over time, traces connect work across an operation, and profiles identify where resources are spent. Start with a hypothesis and evidence rather than changing code because a graph looks unusual.

cards.front: Why does a valid login token not authorize reading any order ID?
cards.back: Authentication identifies the caller. Authorization decides whether that caller may perform this operation on this resource. Every sensitive object access needs the appropriate policy and tenant/ownership scope, even when the ID is hard to guess.

cards.front: Why is escaping or validating input not a substitute for SQL parameterization?
cards.back: Validation checks whether data is acceptable to the application. Parameterization keeps data separate from executable SQL syntax. Use both for their different purposes, and validate permissions separately. Dynamic identifiers such as sort columns require an allowlisted mapping.

cards.front: What is the practical difference between encoding, hashing, and encryption?
cards.back: Encoding changes representation and is reversible without a secret. Hashing produces a digest and is not encryption. Encryption protects confidentiality using a key. Password storage needs a purpose-built salted, work-factored password-hashing scheme, not plain text or a fast general hash.

cards.front: What problem does constructor injection solve, and what problem does it not solve?
cards.back: It makes a class’s dependencies explicit and allows implementations to be supplied by composition. It helps testing and separation of responsibilities. It does not automatically produce good abstractions, thread safety, or correct dependency lifetimes.

cards.front: When should you catch an exception instead of letting it propagate?
cards.back: Catch it where you can recover, translate it into an appropriate boundary outcome, or add useful context while preserving the cause. Do not silently turn failure into success. Use finally or using for cleanup, and preserve the original stack when rethrowing.

cards.front: Why can enumerating the same LINQ query twice do work twice?
cards.back: Many LINQ operators build a deferred sequence that executes when enumerated. Re-enumeration can rerun computation or a database query and observe changed data. Materializing with ToList creates a snapshot at a cost in time and memory.

cards.front: What does ACID describe, and which letter does not mean “all business rules are magically enforced”?
cards.back: Atomicity groups changes; consistency means preserving defined constraints and invariants; isolation controls concurrent interactions; durability covers committed data under the storage contract. The application and schema still must define and enforce the actual business rules.

cards.front: What do a table, row, column, primary key, and foreign key represent?
cards.back: A table stores one kind of fact, a row is one instance, and columns are its attributes. A primary key identifies a row. A foreign key links to an allowed referenced key. SQL queries describe a desired result set; the engine chooses an execution plan.

cards.front: What is the difference between selecting columns and filtering rows?
cards.back: SELECT chooses the output columns and expressions. WHERE decides which source rows survive. AS names an output expression. Listing required columns makes the result contract clearer than SELECT *.

cards.front: Why should mixed AND and OR conditions usually have explicit parentheses?
cards.back: AND binds more tightly than OR. Parentheses state the intended grouping and make review safer. WHERE retains only rows whose predicate is TRUE; FALSE and UNKNOWN do not pass.

cards.front: Why is TOP (2) without ORDER BY not “the two newest rows”?
cards.back: Limiting rows does not define which rows come first. Use ORDER BY for the intended order and a unique tie-breaker for deterministic results. SQL Server uses TOP or OFFSET/FETCH; SQLite uses LIMIT.

cards.front: Why does WHERE city <> 'Oslo' omit a row whose city is NULL?
cards.back: Comparisons with NULL produce UNKNOWN rather than TRUE or FALSE. WHERE keeps only TRUE. Test missing values with IS NULL or IS NOT NULL; use COALESCE only when a replacement matches the business meaning.

cards.front: What is the difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(column)?
cards.back: COUNT(*) counts result rows. COUNT(column) counts rows where that expression is not NULL. SUM and AVG generally ignore NULL inputs; an empty qualifying set yields NULL for SUM and AVG but zero for COUNT.

cards.front: When should a condition be in WHERE versus HAVING?
cards.back: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping. GROUP BY defines one result row per grouping key. HAVING filters the resulting groups, often using an aggregate. SELECT nonaggregated columns must be compatible with the grouping rules.

cards.front: What does INNER JOIN produce when one customer has three matching orders?
cards.back: It produces one result row for each matching customer-order pair, so that customer appears three times. A join combines related rows; it does not automatically return one row per entity or remove duplicates.

cards.front: Why can a WHERE filter on the right table turn a LEFT JOIN into inner-join-like behavior?
cards.back: LEFT JOIN supplies NULL right-side columns for unmatched left rows. A right-side comparison in WHERE often rejects those NULL rows. Put a matching-condition filter in ON when the left rows must remain even without qualifying matches.

cards.front: Why is SUM(Orders.total_cents) wrong after joining orders to multiple order lines?
cards.back: The order’s total repeats once per matching line. Summing at that expanded grain counts some orders more than once. Aggregate at the intended grain before joining, or sum line amounts when that is the actual measure.

cards.front: When is EXISTS clearer than joining and then using DISTINCT?
cards.back: Use EXISTS when you only need to know whether at least one related row exists. It preserves the outer query’s grain without emitting one row per match. NOT EXISTS asks whether no qualifying match exists and avoids the NULL trap of many NOT IN expressions.

cards.front: Does a common table expression automatically cache or materialize its result?
cards.back: No. A CTE names a query expression for the immediately following statement. It improves structure and readability; materialization and repeated work depend on the engine and plan. Use a temporary table when you specifically need stored intermediate results and accept its costs.

cards.front: How do you count paid orders and pending orders in the same grouped query?
cards.back: Use a conditional expression inside an aggregate, for example SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END). CASE chooses a value; it is an expression, not a general procedural control-flow block.

cards.front: How do you select the latest order for each customer without losing the order’s other columns?
cards.back: Assign ROW_NUMBER over each customer partition ordered by date descending and a unique ID descending, then keep rn = 1 in an outer query. GROUP BY with MAX(date) alone does not identify every other column from the latest row.

cards.front: Why specify ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW for a running total?
cards.back: It explicitly sums from the first row through the current row in the window’s sequence. A deterministic order plus a ROWS frame gives row-by-row accumulation. Default frames and peer rows can produce surprising totals when ordering values tie.

cards.front: What does a foreign key guarantee, and what does it not guarantee?
cards.back: It enforces that a non-null referencing value matches an allowed parent key. It does not automatically mean one-to-one, create every helpful index, or enforce unrelated business rules. Nullability and uniqueness define additional parts of the relationship.

cards.front: What should you verify before running UPDATE or DELETE?
cards.back: Confirm the database and intended rows, preview with SELECT using the same predicate, choose a safe transaction boundary, and verify affected-row count. Without WHERE, every qualifying table row can be changed or removed. Practice only in the isolated toy database.

cards.front: What is the difference between COMMIT and ROLLBACK?
cards.back: COMMIT makes the transaction’s changes permanent under the database’s durability contract. ROLLBACK abandons its uncommitted changes. A transaction groups related database operations; it does not automatically make external HTTP or email effects atomic.

cards.front: How does a parameterized query prevent an input string from becoming SQL syntax?
cards.back: The command text defines the query structure, while parameter values are supplied separately through the database driver. The engine treats the bound value as data. Do not build SQL by concatenating untrusted input; use fixed allowlisted mappings for identifiers that cannot be parameters.

cards.front: Why can an index on (customer_id, ordered_on) help an equality-plus-date-range query?
cards.back: The index groups rows by customer first, then orders dates within each customer. Equality narrows to one customer’s region, and a date range narrows within it. Whether the optimizer uses it depends on data, selectivity, output columns, and cost.

cards.front: Why is a half-open date range often preferable to applying a function to every stored date?
cards.back: A predicate that compares an indexed column directly to bounds is often easier to use for an index search. Wrapping the column in a function can block that access path. Verify the actual plan and row counts; sargable syntax does not guarantee a seek or a fast query.

cards.front: Does BEGIN TRANSACTION make every read-then-write business decision safe?
cards.back: No. The isolation level and constraints determine which concurrent interleavings are allowed. Use an atomic conditional update, appropriate locking, optimistic version checks, or Serializable as the invariant requires. Retry conflicts deliberately and re-read the state.

cards.front: How is a database deadlock different from ordinary blocking?
cards.back: Blocking can resolve when the owner releases a resource. A deadlock is a cycle: each participant waits for a resource held by another in the cycle. SQL Server can choose a victim and roll it back. Retry the whole transaction with bounded backoff when safe.

cards.front: What does a keyset cursor store, and why does it need a unique tie-breaker?
cards.back: It stores the last seen ordering values, then asks for rows after that position. A unique tie-breaker makes the order total, so equal timestamps do not create ambiguous page boundaries. Offset skips a count of rows and can become costly or shift under concurrent changes.

cards.front: What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL?
cards.back: UNION combines compatible result sets and removes duplicate complete rows. UNION ALL keeps duplicates and avoids that deduplication requirement. Use ALL when duplicates are meaningful or the inputs are known to be disjoint.
